headlines.title: Woman dies after suspected Richmond arson, bringing death toll to 4
headlines.description: The 33-year-old woman who was critically injured in a house fire allegedly set by her brother on Tuesday has died, the police department said on Saturday. Police said Sergio Rivera-Vega was accused of starting the fire at a home located along the 200 block of 15th Street on Tuesday night. The blaze killed Rivera-Vega’s 47-year-old father and his 5-year-old nephew, his 2-year-old niece and now his 33-year-old sister. Rivera-Vega lived in the home. Police said a motive for the alleged arson is still under investigation. “Our investigators, their number one goal is to figure out why this happened, why this person would do this to their family,” England said. “That is what everybody wants to know.” Richmond Aug 20 Richmond Aug 19 The day of the incident, firefighters had responded to a fire nearby at about 8:15 p.m. After that fire was under control at about 8:45 p.m., bystanders alerted them of another fire at a nearby home, which is the one Rivera-Vega allegedly started, according to authorities. The second fire was under control by about 9:25 p.m., according to officials. Three of the victims were taken to the hospital, where they died. The suspect’s father died at the scene. Police said all of the victims were injured or killed by the fire, and there is no evidence that they were shot or stabbed before the alleged arson.

headlines.title: North Beach closes temporarily after fishing vessel runs aground
headlines.description: North Beach closed temporarily on Saturday after a fishing vessel, with approximately 1,000 gallons of diesel onboard, ran aground on Friday, Point Reyes National Seashore said. The U.S. Coast Guard said Lake Bay, the 58-foot fishing vessel, ran aground on Friday morning in Point Reyes National Seashore. They said the vessel has a maximum fuel capacity of 2,800 gallons and is reported to have approximately 1,000 gallons of diesel onboard. Point Reyes National Seashore said the National Park Service is coordinating with the U.S. Coast Guard Southwest District, NOAA and Marin County Fire while the Coast Guard works to find a contractor to remove the fuel from the vessel. Authorities added no injuries or fuel leaks have been reported. Authorities said visitors are asked to stay clear of North Beach during the closure to ensure first responders work safely and without interference.

headlines.title: Traffic alerts: I-80 Carquinez Bridge closure, limited Highway 101 access in SF
headlines.description: Construction projects on both sides of the Bay this weekend are expected to cause delays for motorists. Here’s what to know about the projects and how to plan ahead. Westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 to shut down Caltrans will close the westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 for 53 hours starting Friday night as crews work on a deck rehabilitation project. The closure will start at 10 p.m. and continue through the weekend. It is scheduled to end by 3 a.m. Monday. The eastbound direction of the bridge will remain open. The San Francisco Bay Ferry said it would provide additional ferry trips Saturday and Sunday on the Vallejo route during the westbound closure. The exact closure will be westbound I-80 between the east end of the bridge and start of the westbound off-ramp to Pomona Street, from Sonoma Boulevard, Sequoia Avenue, Magazine Street and Lincoln Road. Below is a map of the closure: Detours during weekend Carquinez Bridge closure Motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento can take the following alternate routes: Detour for westbound I-80 traffic (before Exit 4): Take exit 40 to merge onto southbound Interstate 680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Highway 4 Continue on westbound Highway 4 Take exit 1B, merge onto westbound I-80 To completely avoid the Carquinez Bridge closure, motorists can use westbound I-680. Regional detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Detour for southbound Highway 29 traffic: Detour to Curtola Parkway and stay in the through lane at the Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street intersection to merge onto eastbound Interstate 780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound I-80 Detour for South Vallejo/Carquinez Heights traffic: Detour to northbound Highway 29 (Sonoma Boulevard) Make a right turn onto Lemon Street Continue on Lemon Street and make a right turn at Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street to merge onto eastbound I-780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Hwy. 4 Continue on westbound Hwy. 4 Take exit 1B to merge onto westbound I-80 Local detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Limited Highway 101 access in San Francisco Starting Friday at 11 p.m., Caltrans will close two lanes in each direction of the Highway 101 Bayshore Freeway (Hospital Curve) area in San Francisco and expects to keep them closed until 6 a.m. Monday. The impacted portion of Highway 101 will be between Cesar Chavez and 17th streets so Caltrans can work on Hospital Curve rehabilitation, which is part of a longer-term project that started in 2025. Another closure is planned for Sept. 4-7. How to avoid Highway 101 traffic Caltrans is suggesting Interstate 280 or public transportation as an option as they shutter the lanes to work on the median near Hospital Curve. Bay City News contributed to this report. San Francisco Aug 20 Transportation Jul 20

headlines.title: Stretch of Hwy. 1 reopens as crews continue to battle Timber Fire near Big Sur
headlines.description: Caltrans announced Saturday the reopening of a 10-mile stretch of Highway 1 in Monterey County following support of the Timber Fire emergency response. Authorities said the stretch was opened as of 1 p.m. Caltrans warns drivers to be cautious or use Highway 101 as an alternative route. According to Cal Fire, the Timber Fire in Monterey County burned 8,665 acres and was 29% contained as of Saturday. According to the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office, the evacuation order for MRY-F027-B was downgraded to an evacuation warning, zone MRY-F028 was divided into zones A, B, C, and D; MRY-F028-A, which includes areas west of Partington Bridge, was downgraded to an evacuation warning. Authorities said the zone MRY-F028-C remains under evacuation order and zone MRY-F029 was upgraded to an evacuation order. Besides those changes, the sheriff’s office said all of the other evacuation orders and warnings remain under effect. Big Sur Aug 14 Monterey County Aug 12 Monterey County Aug 11 Timber Fire in Monterey County nears 3,000 acres with 5% containment

headlines.title: San Jose mayor adopts German shepherd for a day
headlines.description: On Saturday, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan adopted a German shepherd for the day. Mahan brought the German shepherd, named Sinatra, to public events as his official “paw-licy” officer. Sinatra joined the mayor at a cleanup event and even hit the South Bay Run club. The mayor says he is trying to bring attention to shelter animals in need of good homes. Animal Care and Services say the city-run shelter is currently at capacity, with officials urging residents to adopt or foster.

headlines.title: New York passes San Francisco as top tech market
headlines.description: New numbers show the job market is growing in the South Bay even as New York has taken a bigger bite out of the Bay Area’s tech workforce. Commercial real estate firm Cboe Global Markets says for the first time ever, New York City has surpassed San Francisco in total tech jobs. Those tech jobs gave the Bay Area a boost in the latest state jobs report. It shows the artificial intelligence boom is largely responsible for the South Bay adding thousands of new jobs in July, even as California overall lost 20,000 jobs. Scott Budman examines the latest figures in his video report above.

headlines.title: Navigation center workers accused of harboring man who allegedly shot SF police officer
headlines.description: Two employees of a San Francisco navigation center were accused of intentionally hiding a man after he allegedly shot a police officer, authorities said on Friday. In May, San Francisco police say the suspect, Norris Reed III, led officers on a short chase, crashed his car, and then started shooting. Officer Brittney Taylor was shot multiple times and was seriously injured. After the shooting, police say Reed ran into the Five Keys Navigation Center, where he was ultimately arrested. However, investigators now say two workers of Five Keys attempted to hide Reed from authorities. In court filings, prosecutors claim one employee let Reed III into the facility and the other was heard on a security camera saying, “don’t call the police.” San Francisco Jun 1 San Francisco Jun 3 In a statement, the nonprofit shelter contradicts that account, saying workers were trying to de-escalate the situation and evacuate people after Reed III flashed a gun. The full statement reads: “We find these allegations deeply troubling and sincerely hope they are not true. What we do know is the following: During a shift change, an individual entered the facility grounds and attempted to enter the main building. A staff member stopped him at the door. The individual then displayed two firearms and instructed the staff member not to call the police. Our staff immediately began evacuating the premises and contacted the site director by phone. While continuing to engage and de-escalate the individual, staff informed the director that he was requesting a jacket. The director instructed staff to provide the jacket—and anything else he requested—to keep the situation calm. Meanwhile, staff safely evacuated approximately 125 individuals from the facility. Law enforcement arrived shortly after the individual entered the premises. Staff were therefore confident that the police were already aware of the situation, allowing them to temporarily comply with the individual’s instruction not to call while they focused on de-escalation and evacuation. Staff successfully moved the individual out of the building and into the gated exterior area. Once he was outside and the building had been fully evacuated, staff notified law enforcement of his location. This was an extremely dangerous situation that could have resulted in serious injuries. Through calm and deliberate action, our staff prevented the armed individual from entering the building, protected and evacuated approximately 125 people, and helped bring the situation to a peaceful conclusion. Most importantly, no one was injured, and the individual was arrested without further incident.”

headlines.title: Auction features work of legendary Bay Area photographer Michael Zagaris
headlines.description: From Friday through Sunday, work from legendary Bay Area photographer Michael Zagaris will be up for sale through Heritage Auctions. Zagaris has covered some of the biggest events in Bay Area sports and music history. The work for sale includes photographs of Joe Montana and Bill Walsh, along with jerseys from Montana, John Taylor, Ronnie Lott, and Dwight Clark. The collection also spans his work with the A’s, the Rolling Stones and The Who. Raj Mathai talked to Zagaris about the auction. Watch the full interview in the video above.

headlines.title: Palo Alto prepares to audit Flock camera system amid questions over data access
headlines.description: Another Bay Area city is set to wade into the growing controversy over Flock Safety cameras. Palo Alto said it’s preparing to audit its Flock camera system after learning data had been shared through a nationwide network despite local policies limiting who could access it. Law enforcement officials say the automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are critical to public safety, but critics argue they are a dangerous invasion of privacy and are abused by law enforcement. Palo Alto’s independent police auditor, the OIR Group, is expected to review the city’s rules around data sharing, outside access and data retention, as well as how the camera technology is being used. “Our audit is really intended to ensure that if there is misuse, that misuse is immediately identified through internal audits, through other guardrails, training, limitations as to who gets access to the information,” said Michael Gennaco with the OIR Group. The Palo Alto City Council is expected to finalize the scope of the independent audit Monday before deciding what, if anything, should change about the city’s use of the cameras. Brentwood Aug 17 Technology Aug 13 East Bay Jul 31 The audit comes as a handful of other Bay Area communities rethink their relationship with Flock. Some cities have ended their contracts altogether, while others have decided to scale back use. In a statement, Palo Alto’s police chief said the cameras have provided a significant public safety benefit. “ALPR has been a tremendous investigative tool,” the statement read. “It has helped us solve cases, recover stolen vehicles and property, apprehend wanted individuals, and safely locate missing and suicidal persons. I am confident that our officers are using the technology responsibly and to good effect.” Critics of the cameras disagree. “We want to make sure that value isn’t overridden by the lack of trust in misuse of the data,” Gennaco said. In addressing some of the concerns surrounding how the data is used, Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley said, “We don’t own the data. Our customers do. We don’t work with ICE. The customer chooses whom to share that data with. So I’ve found that once people see the truth, they go, ‘This feels like a very good trade-off. But at the end of the day, we have to find a society where safety and privacy can coexist.” Langley said he also supports regulation, including rules around data retention and accountability. “We give power to those who are entitled and ask them to keep us safe, and the accountability has to come with that,” he said. “When I look at regulation, I say there are a couple of things we have to get right. we have to decide how long this data should live, whether it’s seven days, 30 days or a year.”

headlines.title: Bay Area man's proposal aims to remove taxes on restaurant meals
headlines.description: A Bay Area man is proposing eliminating taxes on restaurant meals and wants voters to weigh in if the legislature does not act. If passed, the proposal would mean cities and the state would lose valuable tax revenue. Damian Trujillo takes a closer look. Watch his report in the video above.

headlines.title: ‘So rewarding': Sunnyvale woman hopes her animal adoption adventure inspires others
headlines.description: Diane Foxen’s Sunnyvale home is not just filled with animals, it’s filled with love. The ICU nurse is extra busy these days nursing tuxedo kittens back to health. “It is so rewarding to take care of them, to see them go from this little sick kitten or small kitten that doesn’t know how to eat yet to this big, feisty, running around these guys, playing, loving, purring, and ready for their next adventure in life so that you can start your next adventure,” Foxen said. Foxen’s own adventure started when her son grew up and moved away. She said she became depressed due to empty nest syndrome and the COVID-19 lockdown. But then a cat named Orion filled that empty space. “Orion was one of those foster kittens,” Foxen said. “He was super, super sick, and he just showed his resilience and the will to survive and showed me how precious life is.” The bond convinced Foxen to be even more adventurous. She and Orion completed a 900-mile bike-a-thon from Canada to California to raise money for Humane Society Silicon Valley. “He was my little tent partner,” Foxen said. “He was my camping partner. That bond just kind of filled that empty space, gave back to me what I gave back to him.” Foxen said she hopes her story inspires people to take part in the Clear The Shelters animal adoption campaign and shows that adoption is a journey taken one step at a time. Community Aug 3 clear the shelters Aug 14 “If you’re on the fence about adopting, foster first,” she said. “It’s a great way to see, ‘Will this fit into my lifestyle?'” Max Piekarus with Humane Society Silicon Valley said fostering helps more animals get adopted. “Oftentimes you’ll have someone foster and fall in love, like Diane did with Orion, and adopt, which is always a great outcome, but ideally one person will foster until they’re ready for adoption.” Foxen pointed out that love requires responsibility, like making sure pets are spayed or neutered so they don’t add to the population of homeless animals. Then, enjoy the adventure. “Don’t be afraid to try to foster and to adopt and make space for those animals that are helpless and looking for someone to love them,” she said.

headlines.title: Farmers hope new steam technology will eliminate use of pesticides
headlines.description: Farmworkers have claimed for years that contact with pesticides has left them battling cancer, neurological disorders and other ailments. A new technology aims to weed out pesticides by turning to steam. National advocacy group Farmworker Justice has been fighting the use of toxic pesticides on crops for years. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that roughly 10,000 to 20,000 farmworkers suffer from acute pesticide poisonings every year. Shinta Kawahara Family Farms in Santa Cruz County believes it has found a better way. The organic farm is testing new technology that uses high pressure steam, instead of toxic fumigants, to prep the soil before a plant or seed goes into the ground. Rod Koda’s farm was one of the first in the nation to begin testing the steam technology, and he believes it’s working. “I don’t have the plant mortality, and the fruit would be bigger because the plant is not stressed, the root is not stressed,” Koda said. Researchers say the steam serves as a herbicide and reduces plant disease by 70%, killing the soil pests. The strawberry commission is on board, as is David Sanford, the agriculture commissioner in Santa Cruz County. “It’s early on in their field trials, but the work that we’ve seen so far is pretty promising and it shows a lot of potential,” Sanford said. “It needs research. It needs work.” The hope is to one day limit or eliminate the need for pesticides on crops. “This is the first season and it’s really exciting,” Koda said.
